title: Git Mastery: From Fundamentals to Advanced Workflows
subtitle: Learn Git from first commit to advanced branching, rebasing, collaboration, recovery, automation, and real-world team workflows.

chapters.title: Git Fundamentals
chapters.summary: Understand version control, Git's architecture, repositories, commits, the staging area, and the basic development workflow.

sections.title: What Is Git?
sections.content:
Git is a distributed version control system designed to track changes in source code and other files. Unlike a simple backup system, Git records a history of changes so developers can inspect, compare, revert, branch, merge, and collaborate safely.

Git is **distributed**, which means a cloned repository contains the complete repository history rather than depending on a single central server for normal version-control operations.

A typical workflow is: modify files → inspect changes → stage changes → create a commit → share commits with a remote repository.

callout.title: Git vs GitHub
callout.message: Git is the version-control system. GitHub, GitLab, and Bitbucket are services that host Git repositories and provide collaboration features.

diagram.title: Basic Git Workflow
diagram.code:
flowchart LR
  W[Working Directory] -->|git add| S[Staging Area]
  S -->|git commit| L[Local Repository]
  L -->|git push| R[Remote Repository]
  R -->|git pull/fetch| L

codeExample.title: Create Your First Repository
codeExample.code:
mkdir git-demo
cd git-demo
git init
echo "Hello Git" > README.md
git add README.md
git commit -m "Initial commit"
codeExample.explanation: `git init` creates a Git repository. `git add` places a change into the staging area, and `git commit` permanently records the staged snapshot in the repository history.

keyTakeaways: Git tracks changes as a history of commits.
Git repositories contain their own local history.
The normal workflow moves changes from working directory to staging area and then into a commit.

interactiveQuiz.question: What is Git primarily used for?
interactiveQuiz.explanation: Git is a distributed version control system used to track changes, maintain history, create branches, and collaborate on projects.

sections.title: Working Directory, Staging Area, and Repository
sections.content:
Git conceptually separates your project into three important areas. The **working directory** contains the files you are currently editing. The **staging area**, also called the index, contains changes selected for the next commit. The **repository** contains committed snapshots.

This separation lets you create focused commits. For example, if you modify three files but only one change is ready, you can stage only that file and commit it.

diagram.title: Git's Three Areas
diagram.code:
flowchart LR
  A[Working Directory] -->|git add| B[Staging Area / Index]
  B -->|git commit| C[Git Repository]
  C -->|git restore| A
  B -->|git restore --staged| A

codeExample.title: Stage Selectively
codeExample.code:
git status
git add src/auth.js
git status
git commit -m "Add authentication validation"
codeExample.explanation: Only `src/auth.js` is staged, so the commit can contain that logical change without automatically including unrelated modifications.

keyTakeaways: Staging is a preparation step, not the same as committing.
Use selective staging to keep commits focused and reviewable.
The repository contains committed snapshots rather than an editable working copy.

interactiveQuiz.question: Which Git area contains changes selected for the next commit?
interactiveQuiz.explanation: The staging area, or index, contains changes that have been selected using commands such as `git add` and will be included in the next commit.

sections.title: Initializing and Inspecting Repositories
sections.content: Use `git init` when starting version control in an existing directory. Use `git clone` when obtaining an existing repository. The `git status` command is one of the most frequently used Git commands because it explains the current state of tracked, modified, staged, and untracked files.

codeExample.title: Repository Inspection
codeExample.code:
git init
git status
git log --oneline
git branch
git remote -v
codeExample.explanation: These commands help establish whether the directory is a repository, what changes exist, what commits are present, which branches exist, and which remote repositories are configured.

callout.title: Use git status Frequently
callout.message: Running git status before staging, committing, switching branches, or cleaning files prevents many common Git mistakes.

keyTakeaways: `git init` creates a repository while `git clone` copies an existing repository.
`git status` is the primary command for understanding your current working state.

interactiveQuiz.question: Which command creates a new Git repository in the current directory?
interactiveQuiz.explanation: `git init` initializes a new `.git` directory and turns the current directory into a Git repository.

sections.title: Commits and Repository History
sections.content:
A commit represents a recorded snapshot of the project's state. Each commit has an identifier, author information, timestamp, message, parent relationship, and references to the content tree.

Good commit messages describe the intent of the change. Prefer small, logical commits such as `Fix token expiration validation` instead of vague messages such as `changes`.

codeExample.title: Inspect Commit History
codeExample.code:
git log
git log --oneline --decorate --graph --all
git show HEAD
git show HEAD~1
codeExample.explanation: `git log` displays history, while `git show` displays the details of a particular commit. `HEAD~1` refers to the first parent of the current commit.

keyTakeaways: Commits form a directed history through parent relationships.
Useful commit messages communicate intent.
Graph views make branches and merges easier to understand.

interactiveQuiz.question: What does HEAD normally identify?
options: The currently checked-out commit or branch reference
interactiveQuiz.explanation: HEAD is Git's symbolic reference to the currently checked-out position, commonly pointing to the current branch, which in turn points to a commit.

chapters.title: Staging, Commits, and Undoing Changes
chapters.summary: Master staging techniques, diff inspection, commit creation, restoring files, and safely undoing changes.

sections.title: Understanding git diff
sections.content: `git diff` compares your working tree with the staging area. `git diff --staged` compares the staged snapshot with the current commit. These commands are essential before committing because they let you verify exactly what will be recorded.

codeExample.title: Inspect Changes
codeExample.code:
git diff
git diff --staged
git diff HEAD
git diff HEAD~1 HEAD
codeExample.explanation: `git diff` shows unstaged changes. `git diff --staged` shows staged changes. `git diff HEAD` compares the entire working state against HEAD.

keyTakeaways: Review `git diff` before staging.
Review `git diff --staged` before committing.
`git diff HEAD` combines the comparison against the current commit.

interactiveQuiz.question: Which command shows changes currently staged for commit?
interactiveQuiz.explanation: `git diff --staged` compares the staging area against HEAD and therefore shows what the next commit would contain.

sections.title: Restoring and Unstaging Files
sections.content: Modern Git provides `git restore` for restoring working-tree files and removing changes from the staging area. `git restore file.js` discards unstaged modifications to that file, while `git restore --staged file.js` removes it from the staging area without discarding its working-tree changes.

callout.title: Discarded Changes Can Be Lost
callout.message: `git restore file.js` can permanently discard uncommitted modifications to that file. Inspect the diff first if the changes matter.

codeExample.title: Restore and Unstage
codeExample.code:
git restore app.js
git restore --staged app.js
git restore --source=HEAD~1 app.js
codeExample.explanation: The first command restores the working file from the index. The second removes it from staging. The third restores the file from another commit.

keyTakeaways: `git restore --staged` unstages without discarding the working copy.
`git restore` can discard working-tree changes.
Use explicit source commits when restoring historical versions.

interactiveQuiz.question: What does `git restore --staged file.js` do?
options: Unstages the file while keeping working-tree changes
interactiveQuiz.explanation: The command removes the file from the index while leaving the modifications in the working tree.

sections.title: Amending Commits
sections.content:
When you have just created a commit and discover a small mistake, `git commit --amend` can replace the current commit with a corrected version. It is useful for fixing the latest commit message or adding forgotten changes.

Amending changes the commit identity. Avoid rewriting a commit that has already been shared when other developers may depend on its original history.

codeExample.title: Amend the Latest Commit
codeExample.code:
git add forgotten-file.js
git commit --amend --no-edit

git commit --amend -m "Correct commit message"
codeExample.explanation: `--no-edit` keeps the existing message. Supplying `-m` replaces it. Both operations create a replacement commit for the previous HEAD.

keyTakeaways: Amend is ideal for fixing the latest local commit.
Amending changes the commit hash.
Be careful when rewriting history that others have already pulled.

interactiveQuiz.question: What is a common use for `git commit --amend`?
options: Fix or extend the latest commit
interactiveQuiz.explanation: `git commit --amend` replaces the latest commit, allowing you to correct its message or add additional staged changes.

sections.title: Understanding git reset
sections.content:
`git reset` moves the current branch reference and can also modify the staging area and working tree depending on its mode. `--soft` moves HEAD while keeping changes staged. `--mixed`, the default, moves HEAD and resets the index while keeping working-tree changes. `--hard` resets HEAD, the index, and working tree.

Reset is powerful and should be used carefully, particularly on shared branches.

codeExample.title: Reset Modes
codeExample.code:
git reset --soft HEAD~1
git reset --mixed HEAD~1
git reset --hard HEAD~1
codeExample.explanation: `--soft` preserves staged changes, `--mixed` preserves them only in the working tree, and `--hard` discards tracked working-tree and staging changes that differ from the target.

callout.title: Use --hard Carefully
callout.message: `git reset --hard` can remove uncommitted tracked changes. Make sure important work is committed, stashed, or otherwise backed up before using it.

keyTakeaways: Soft reset preserves changes in the index.
Mixed reset is the default and unstages changes.
Hard reset can discard local tracked changes.

interactiveQuiz.question: Which reset mode keeps changes staged after moving HEAD?
interactiveQuiz.explanation: `git reset --soft` changes HEAD but leaves the index and working tree untouched, so the changes remain staged.

chapters.title: Branches and Parallel Development
chapters.summary: Learn how Git branches work, create feature branches, switch safely, track remote branches, and structure parallel development.

sections.title: How Git Branches Work
sections.content:
A Git branch is essentially a movable reference pointing to a commit. Creating a branch is cheap because Git does not duplicate the entire project. As new commits are created, the branch reference advances.

The special reference `HEAD` identifies the currently checked-out position.

diagram.title: Branch References
diagram.code:
gitGraph
  commit id: "A"
  commit id: "B"
  branch feature
  checkout feature
  commit id: "C"
  checkout main
  commit id: "D"

codeExample.title: Create and Switch Branches
codeExample.code:
git branch feature/login
git switch feature/login

git switch -c feature/profile
codeExample.explanation: `git branch` creates a branch without switching to it. `git switch` changes the current branch, and `git switch -c` creates and checks out a new branch.

keyTakeaways: Branches are lightweight references to commits.
Feature branches isolate work from the main line.
`git switch -c` is a convenient modern command for creating and switching.

interactiveQuiz.question: What does a Git branch primarily represent?
options: A movable reference to a commit
interactiveQuiz.explanation: A branch is a reference that points to a commit and moves forward as new commits are created on that branch.

sections.title: git switch and git checkout
sections.content:
`git checkout` historically handled both branch switching and file restoration, which can make commands ambiguous. Modern Git provides `git switch` for branch operations and `git restore` for file restoration.

`checkout` remains valid and is widely encountered in existing projects, but `switch` and `restore` communicate intent more clearly.

codeExample.title: Modern Branch Commands
codeExample.code:
git switch main
git switch -c feature/search
git branch --show-current
codeExample.explanation: These commands explicitly communicate branch operations and make scripts and workflows easier to understand.

keyTakeaways: `git switch` is focused on branch changes.
`git restore` is focused on restoring files.
`git checkout` is still valid but has multiple historical responsibilities.

interactiveQuiz.question: Which modern command is specifically designed for switching branches?
interactiveQuiz.explanation: `git switch` was introduced to provide a clearer interface for changing and creating branches.

sections.title: Tracking Branches
sections.content:
A local branch can track a remote branch. This relationship allows commands such as `git pull` and `git push` to infer the upstream branch. You can configure it explicitly with `git push -u origin feature/login`.

Tracking information is metadata about branch relationships; it does not copy commits by itself.

codeExample.title: Set an Upstream Branch
codeExample.code:
git switch -c feature/login
git push -u origin feature/login
git branch -vv
codeExample.explanation: The `-u` option establishes the remote branch as the upstream for the local branch. `git branch -vv` displays tracking relationships.

keyTakeaways: Upstream configuration connects a local branch with a remote-tracking branch.
`git push -u` commonly establishes the relationship during the first push.

interactiveQuiz.question: What does `git push -u origin feature/login` commonly configure?
interactiveQuiz.explanation: The `-u` option sets the remote branch as the upstream branch for the local branch.

sections.title: Listing, Renaming, and Deleting Branches
sections.content:
Git provides commands for managing branch references. Local branches can be listed with `git branch`, renamed with `git branch -m`, and deleted with `git branch -d`. Remote branches can be removed using `git push origin --delete branch-name`.

Deleting a branch does not automatically delete commits if those commits are still reachable through another reference.

codeExample.title: Branch Maintenance
codeExample.code:
git branch
git branch -a
git branch -m old-name new-name
git branch -d feature/login
git push origin --delete feature/login
codeExample.explanation: These commands inspect local and remote-tracking branches, rename a local branch, delete a merged local branch, and remove a branch from the remote.

keyTakeaways: Use `-d` for safe deletion of merged branches.
Use `-D` only when intentionally forcing deletion.
Remote branch deletion is a push operation.

interactiveQuiz.question: Which command safely deletes a merged local branch?
interactiveQuiz.explanation: `git branch -d` performs a safety check and normally refuses to delete a branch whose commits have not been merged.

chapters.title: Merging, Rebasing, and Conflict Resolution
chapters.summary: Understand merge commits, fast-forward merges, rebasing, conflict resolution, and when to choose each integration strategy.

sections.title: Merging Branches
sections.content: Merging integrates the history of one branch into another. A fast-forward merge occurs when the target branch has not diverged and can simply move its reference forward. When branches have diverged, Git may create a merge commit that records both parent histories.

diagram.title: Merge Integration
diagram.code:
flowchart LR
  A[main] --> B[Common Commit]
  B --> C[main commits]
  B --> D[feature commits]
  C --> M[Merge Commit]
  D --> M

codeExample.title: Merge a Feature
codeExample.code:
git switch main
git merge feature/login
git log --oneline --graph --decorate --all
codeExample.explanation: The feature branch is merged into the currently checked-out `main` branch. Git chooses an appropriate merge strategy based on the relationship between the branches.

keyTakeaways: A merge preserves the original branch histories.
Fast-forward merging does not create an additional merge commit.
A merge commit can have two or more parents.

interactiveQuiz.question: What is a fast-forward merge?
options: A merge that deletes the source branch
A merge where the target reference can simply advance
A merge that always creates two commits
A merge performed only on GitHub
interactiveQuiz.explanation: When the target branch is an ancestor of the source branch, Git can move the target reference forward without creating a merge commit.

sections.title: Rebasing
sections.content:
Rebase moves or replays commits onto a new base. It can create a cleaner, linear-looking history, but it rewrites commit identities because the replayed commits are new commits.

A common workflow is rebasing a feature branch onto the latest `main` before opening a pull request.

codeExample.title: Rebase a Feature Branch
codeExample.code:
git switch feature/login
git fetch origin
git rebase origin/main
codeExample.explanation: Git temporarily removes the feature commits, updates the base to `origin/main`, and replays those feature commits on top of it.

callout.title: Rebase Rewrites History
callout.message: Do not casually rebase commits that other developers have already based work on. Shared history rewriting can force collaborators to reconcile divergent commit identities.

keyTakeaways: Rebase creates new commit identities for replayed commits.
Rebase can produce a linear history.
Avoid rewriting public history unless the team explicitly agrees.

interactiveQuiz.question: Why does rebasing change commit hashes?
options: Replayed commits have different parent relationships and therefore new identities
interactiveQuiz.explanation: A commit's identity depends on its content and metadata, including its parent. Replaying it onto a different parent creates a different commit.

sections.title: Resolving Merge Conflicts
sections.content:
A conflict occurs when Git cannot automatically reconcile changes, often because different branches modified overlapping lines. Git marks conflicted files with conflict markers such as `<<<<<<<`, `=======`, and `>>>>>>>`.

The resolution process is: inspect conflicts → edit the file into the desired final state → stage the resolved file → continue the merge or rebase.

codeExample.title: Resolve a Merge Conflict
codeExample.code:
git status
# edit conflicted files
git add src/app.js
git commit

# During a rebase:
git add src/app.js
git rebase --continue
codeExample.explanation: After resolving the file contents, staging marks the conflict as resolved. During a merge, the next step is normally committing; during a rebase, use `git rebase --continue`.

keyTakeaways: Conflict markers must be removed from the final file.
Git considers a conflict resolved when the corrected file is staged.
`git rebase --abort` can safely cancel an in-progress rebase.

interactiveQuiz.question: What should you normally do after manually resolving a conflicted file?
interactiveQuiz.explanation: Staging the corrected file tells Git that the conflict has been resolved and the file is ready for the merge or rebase to continue.

sections.title: Interactive Rebase
sections.content:
Interactive rebase lets you reorganize, edit, squash, reorder, or drop commits before sharing them. It is particularly useful for cleaning up a feature branch before review.

Commands in an interactive rebase include `pick`, `reword`, `edit`, `squash`, `fixup`, and `drop`.

codeExample.title: Clean Up Recent Commits
codeExample.code:
git rebase -i HEAD~4

# Example todo:
# pick abc123 Add login form
# squash def456 Fix login form
# reword 789abc Add validation
# pick 012def Add tests
codeExample.explanation: The interactive todo list determines how Git should replay the selected commits.

keyTakeaways: Interactive rebase is useful for local history cleanup.
`squash` combines commits while allowing message editing.
`fixup` combines commits while discarding the fixup commit's message.

interactiveQuiz.question: What does `squash` do in an interactive rebase?
options: Combines a commit with the previous commit
interactiveQuiz.explanation: `squash` combines the selected commit with the previous commit and normally opens an editor to construct the resulting commit message.

chapters.title: Remote Repositories and Team Collaboration
chapters.summary: Learn fetch, pull, push, remotes, pull requests, fork-based collaboration, and safe synchronization with shared repositories.

sections.title: Remote Repositories
sections.content:
A remote is a named reference to another Git repository. `origin` is the conventional name assigned to the repository from which a clone was created, but it is only a name and can be changed.

Use `git remote -v` to inspect configured URLs and `git remote add` to add another remote.

codeExample.title: Manage Remotes
codeExample.code:
git remote -v
git remote add upstream https://example.com/team/project.git
git remote set-url origin https://example.com/my/project.git
git remote remove upstream
codeExample.explanation: Remote names are local aliases for repository URLs. A project can have multiple remotes such as `origin` and `upstream`.

keyTakeaways: A remote is a local name pointing to another repository.
`origin` is conventional, not mandatory.
Multiple remotes can be configured.

interactiveQuiz.question: Is `origin` a special Git keyword that must always refer to GitHub?
options: No, it is a conventional remote name
interactiveQuiz.explanation: `origin` is simply the default remote name commonly created by `git clone`. It can point to any compatible Git repository.

sections.title: git fetch
sections.content: `git fetch` downloads new objects and updates remote-tracking references without changing your current working branch. It is useful when you want to inspect incoming changes before integrating them.

codeExample.title: Fetch and Inspect
codeExample.code:
git fetch origin
git log main..origin/main --oneline
git diff main origin/main
codeExample.explanation: Fetching updates `origin/main`. You can then inspect commits and differences before deciding whether to merge or rebase.

keyTakeaways: `git fetch` does not normally modify your working branch.
It updates remote-tracking references such as `origin/main`.
Fetching before integration gives you control over how incoming changes are handled.

interactiveQuiz.question: What is a key property of `git fetch`?
options: It downloads updates without integrating them into the current branch
interactiveQuiz.explanation: `git fetch` downloads remote objects and updates remote-tracking references but does not automatically merge them into your current branch.

sections.title: git pull
sections.content: `git pull` is commonly understood as fetch followed by integration. Depending on configuration, the integration can be a merge or a rebase. Because it combines multiple operations, understanding `fetch` separately is important when precise control is needed.

codeExample.title: Pull With Explicit Strategy
codeExample.code:
git pull --ff-only
git pull --rebase
git fetch origin
git merge origin/main
codeExample.explanation: `--ff-only` refuses non-fast-forward integration, while `--rebase` rebases local commits on top of fetched changes. Fetch plus merge makes the individual steps explicit.

keyTakeaways: `git pull` performs fetching and integration.
Pull behavior can be configured or specified explicitly.
Use `git fetch` when you want to inspect changes before integrating.

interactiveQuiz.question: Why might a developer prefer `git fetch` followed by an explicit merge?
interactiveQuiz.explanation: Separating fetching from integration gives the developer an opportunity to inspect incoming commits and differences before changing the current branch.

sections.title: Pushing Changes
sections.content:
`git push` transfers local commits to a remote repository and updates remote references when permitted. Modern hosting platforms may reject pushes because of branch protection, authentication requirements, or non-fast-forward history.

A push does not normally send every object in your entire repository; Git transfers the objects required to update the remote.

codeExample.title: Push a Branch
codeExample.code:
git push -u origin feature/login
git push
git push --force-with-lease
codeExample.explanation: The first push establishes tracking. A normal push sends new commits. `--force-with-lease` is a safer history-rewrite mechanism than unconditional `--force` because it checks the expected remote state.

callout.title: Prefer --force-with-lease
callout.message: When a history rewrite is genuinely required, prefer `--force-with-lease` because it helps avoid overwriting remote work that you have not seen.

keyTakeaways: Push transfers commits and updates remote references.
Protected branches can reject direct pushes.
`--force-with-lease` is safer than blind `--force`.

interactiveQuiz.question: Why is `--force-with-lease` generally safer than `--force`?
options: It checks that the remote reference is still at the expected state
It creates a backup branch automatically
interactiveQuiz.explanation: `--force-with-lease` checks that the remote branch has not advanced unexpectedly before replacing its history.

sections.title: Pull Requests and Code Review
sections.content:
A pull request is a collaboration mechanism provided by platforms such as GitHub and GitLab. It allows a branch to be reviewed and discussed before integration. A pull request is not itself a Git object; it is a hosting-platform concept built around Git references and commits.

A good pull request is focused, explains the problem and solution, includes tests, and minimizes unrelated changes.
keyTakeaways: Pull requests are platform-level collaboration features.
Small focused pull requests are easier to review.
CI checks and code review can be required before merging.

interactiveQuiz.question: Is a pull request a native Git object?
options: No, it is a collaboration feature provided by hosting platforms
interactiveQuiz.explanation: Git itself provides commits, branches, tags, refs, and other repository concepts. Pull requests are features implemented by services such as GitHub and GitLab.

chapters.title: Stash, Cherry-Pick, Tags, and Releases
chapters.summary: Learn practical tools for temporarily shelving work, selectively transferring commits, marking releases, and managing versions.

sections.title: Temporarily Stashing Work
sections.content:
`git stash` temporarily saves working-tree and staging changes so you can switch context without committing incomplete work. A stash is stored in Git's stash references and can later be applied or popped.

Modern Git also supports `git stash push -m` for descriptive stash messages and `git stash push -u` to include untracked files.

codeExample.title: Stash and Restore Work
codeExample.code:
git stash push -m "WIP login validation"
git switch main
git switch feature/login
git stash list
git stash pop
codeExample.explanation: `stash push` saves the changes. `stash list` shows saved entries, while `stash pop` applies the latest stash and removes it if successful.

keyTakeaways: Stash is useful for temporarily incomplete work.
Use descriptive stash messages when maintaining multiple entries.
Stashes can conflict when applied to changed code.

interactiveQuiz.question: What is the primary purpose of `git stash`?
interactiveQuiz.explanation: Stash temporarily stores changes so you can change branches or context without creating an incomplete commit.

sections.title: Cherry-Picking Commits
sections.content:
`git cherry-pick` applies the changes introduced by selected commits onto the current branch. It is useful when one specific fix is needed without merging an entire branch.

Cherry-picking creates a new commit on the destination branch, so the resulting commit normally has a different hash from the original.

codeExample.title: Apply a Specific Fix
codeExample.code:
git switch release/1.4
git cherry-pick abc1234
codeExample.explanation: Git applies the changes from commit `abc1234` to the current branch and creates a new commit containing those changes.

keyTakeaways: Cherry-pick is useful for selective commit transfer.
The resulting commit is normally a new commit with a different hash.
Cherry-picking can introduce conflicts.

interactiveQuiz.question: What does cherry-pick primarily do?
options: Applies the changes from a selected commit to the current branch
interactiveQuiz.explanation: Cherry-pick takes the changes introduced by one or more commits and applies them to the currently checked-out branch.

sections.title: Tags and Versioning
sections.content: Tags are references used to mark important points in history, commonly releases such as `v1.0.0`. Lightweight tags point directly to an object, while annotated tags store additional metadata such as tagger information, message, and date.

codeExample.title: Create a Release Tag
codeExample.code:
git tag -a v1.0.0 -m "Release 1.0.0"
git tag
git show v1.0.0
git push origin v1.0.0
codeExample.explanation: The annotated tag marks the current commit with release metadata. Tags must be explicitly pushed unless using an appropriate tag push command.

keyTakeaways: Tags are useful for marking releases.
Annotated tags contain metadata and are generally preferred for releases.
Tags are not automatically pushed with ordinary branch pushes.

interactiveQuiz.question: Which command creates an annotated tag?
interactiveQuiz.explanation: The `-a` option creates an annotated tag and `-m` supplies its message.

sections.title: Advanced History Inspection
sections.content: Git history can be queried in many ways. `git log --author`, `--grep`, `--since`, path filters, and graph formatting allow you to locate specific changes. `git blame` identifies the commit associated with each line of a file and can be useful when investigating historical decisions.

codeExample.title: Search Git History
codeExample.code:
git log --oneline --all --grep="authentication"
git log --author="Suriya" --oneline
git log -- src/auth.js
git blame src/auth.js
codeExample.explanation: These commands search commit messages, filter by author, restrict history to a file, and attribute lines to historical commits.

callout.title: Use Blame for Context, Not Blame
callout.message: `git blame` is most useful for finding the commit and author associated with a line so you can inspect the surrounding historical context.

keyTakeaways: Git log can filter history by author, message, date, and path.
`git blame` is a historical attribution tool.
Inspect the associated commit to understand why a line was introduced.

interactiveQuiz.question: What is `git blame` primarily used for?
options: Showing which commit and author last changed each line
interactiveQuiz.explanation: `git blame` annotates lines with information about the commit and author responsible for the latest change to those lines.

chapters.title: Git Recovery and Debugging
chapters.summary: Recover lost commits, inspect reflogs, find regressions with bisect, and safely diagnose difficult repository states.

sections.title: Recovering Work with Reflog
sections.content:
`git reflog` records movements of references such as HEAD and local branches. It can often help recover commits that are no longer reachable through normal branch references, such as after an accidental reset.

Reflog entries are local and are not part of the shared repository history.

codeExample.title: Recover an Accidentally Reset Commit
codeExample.code:
git reflog
# Find the previous HEAD

git branch recovery abc1234
git switch recovery
codeExample.explanation: After locating the desired historical HEAD position in the reflog, creating a new branch at that commit gives the commit a reachable reference again.

callout.title: Reflog Is a Safety Net
callout.message: A commit disappearing from normal branch history does not immediately mean its objects are gone. Reflog can provide a route back while the relevant objects remain available.

keyTakeaways: Reflog records local reference movements.
It is extremely useful after accidental reset or rebase operations.
Reflog is local and should not be treated as a shared backup.

interactiveQuiz.question: What is `git reflog` especially useful for?
interactiveQuiz.explanation: Reflog records local movements of references and can help locate commits that are no longer reachable from current branches.

sections.title: Finding Bugs with git bisect
sections.content: `git bisect` performs a binary search through commit history to locate the commit that introduced a regression. You mark a known bad commit and a known good commit, and Git repeatedly checks out a midpoint. You test that version and tell Git whether it is good or bad.

codeExample.title: Binary Search a Regression
codeExample.code:
git bisect start
git bisect bad
git bisect good v1.0.0

# test the checked-out commit
git bisect good
# or
git bisect bad

git bisect reset
codeExample.explanation: Git narrows the search range by approximately half after every good/bad classification. Once finished, `git bisect reset` returns to the original branch.

keyTakeaways: Bisect is efficient for locating regressions in large histories.
Each classification should accurately reflect whether the tested revision is good or bad.
Automated tests can be used with `git bisect run`.

interactiveQuiz.question: What algorithmic strategy does `git bisect` use?
interactiveQuiz.explanation: Bisect repeatedly halves the range between known good and bad commits, making it a binary search over repository history.

sections.title: Cleaning Untracked Files
sections.content:
`git clean` removes untracked files from the working tree. It can be useful for returning a build directory to a clean state, but it is destructive because untracked files are not recoverable through Git history.

Always use a dry run first with `git clean -n`.

codeExample.title: Preview Before Cleaning
codeExample.code:
git clean -n
git clean -nd
git clean -fd
codeExample.explanation: `-n` previews files, `-d` includes untracked directories, and `-f` performs the deletion. Never use destructive cleanup blindly.

callout.title: Untracked Files Are Not Versioned
callout.message: Git cannot recover an untracked file after `git clean` removes it. Always preview the operation first.

keyTakeaways: `git clean -n` is the safest first step.
Untracked files are outside normal commit history.
Use `.gitignore` to prevent generated files from repeatedly appearing as untracked.

interactiveQuiz.question: What does `git clean -n` do?
options: Shows what would be removed without deleting it
interactiveQuiz.explanation: `-n` means dry run. Git reports what it would remove without actually deleting the files.

sections.title: Detached HEAD
sections.content: A detached HEAD occurs when HEAD points directly to a commit rather than to a branch reference. This is normal when inspecting historical commits or checking out tags. You can make temporary commits in this state, but those commits may become difficult to reach after switching away unless you create a branch.

codeExample.title: Recover Work from Detached HEAD
codeExample.code:
git switch --detach abc1234
# make changes and commit

git switch -c experiment
git log --oneline --decorate
codeExample.explanation: Creating a branch while detached gives the new commits a named reference so they remain easy to find.

keyTakeaways: Detached HEAD is not automatically an error.
It is common when inspecting commits and tags.
Create a branch if you want to preserve new commits made there.

interactiveQuiz.question: What does detached HEAD mean?
options: HEAD points directly to a commit rather than a branch
interactiveQuiz.explanation: In detached HEAD state, HEAD references a commit directly instead of following a branch reference.

chapters.title: Git Configuration, Ignore Rules, and Hooks
chapters.summary: Configure Git, create effective .gitignore rules, use aliases, and understand client-side hooks.

sections.title: Git Configuration
sections.content:
Git configuration exists at multiple levels: system, global, and local repository configuration. Local repository configuration has higher precedence than global configuration.

Common configuration includes user identity, default branch name, editor, aliases, and pull behavior.

codeExample.title: Configure Git Identity
codeExample.code:
git config --global user.name "Suriya"
git config --global user.email "developer@example.com"
git config --global init.defaultBranch main
git config --list --show-origin
codeExample.explanation: Global configuration applies to repositories for the current user. Repository-local configuration can override global settings.

keyTakeaways: Git configuration can exist at multiple scopes.
Local repository configuration can override global settings.
Use `--show-origin` to understand where a configuration value came from.

interactiveQuiz.question: Which configuration generally has higher precedence: local repository configuration or global configuration?
interactiveQuiz.explanation: Repository-local configuration generally overrides global configuration for that repository.

sections.title: .gitignore
sections.content:
The `.gitignore` file defines patterns for files Git should normally leave untracked. Common examples include build output, dependency directories, local environment files, editor metadata, and logs.

Ignoring a file does not remove it from history if it is already tracked. In that case, you need to remove it from the index while optionally keeping it on disk.

codeExample.title: Useful Ignore Rules
codeExample.code:
# .gitignore
node_modules/
dist/
.env
*.log
.vscode/

# Stop tracking an already committed environment file
git rm --cached .env
codeExample.explanation: The patterns ignore common generated or local files. `git rm --cached` removes a tracked file from Git's index while leaving the local file on disk.

keyTakeaways: Ignore rules affect untracked files.
Adding a tracked file to `.gitignore` does not automatically untrack it.
Never commit secrets such as production credentials.

interactiveQuiz.question: What happens if a file is already tracked and you add it to `.gitignore`?
options: It remains tracked until explicitly removed from the index
interactiveQuiz.explanation: `.gitignore` primarily affects untracked files. A tracked file continues to be tracked until removed from the index.

sections.title: Git Aliases
sections.content: Git aliases create shorter commands for frequently used operations. They can improve productivity when used for commands that are stable and easy to remember.

codeExample.title: Create Useful Aliases
codeExample.code:
git config --global alias.co checkout
git config --global alias.st status
git config --global alias.lg "log --oneline --graph --decorate --all"

git st
git lg
codeExample.explanation: Aliases are stored in Git configuration. Shell commands and complex aliases can be created, but keep aliases understandable for team environments.

keyTakeaways: Aliases are configuration conveniences.
Keep important team instructions independent of personal aliases.
Aliases can wrap complex Git commands.

interactiveQuiz.question: Where are Git aliases commonly stored when created with `git config --global`?
options: Only in the repository's object database
In the user's global Git configuration
interactiveQuiz.explanation: The `--global` scope stores the alias in the user's global Git configuration.

sections.title: Git Hooks
sections.content:
Git hooks are scripts triggered by Git lifecycle events. Client-side hooks can run before commits, after commits, before pushes, and during other operations. Teams often use hooks to run formatting, linting, tests, or validation.

Hooks are local by default and are not automatically versioned simply because they exist in `.git/hooks`.

codeExample.title: Simple Pre-Commit Hook
codeExample.code:
# .git/hooks/pre-commit
#!/bin/sh
npm test
if [ $? -ne 0 ]; then
  echo "Tests failed. Commit aborted."
  exit 1
fi
codeExample.explanation: A non-zero exit code from the pre-commit hook prevents the commit. Teams often use hook-management tools when hooks need to be shared consistently.

keyTakeaways: Hooks can enforce local development checks.
Client-side hooks can be bypassed or may not exist on every developer machine.
Critical validation should also run in CI.

interactiveQuiz.question: Which hook commonly runs before a commit is created?
interactiveQuiz.explanation: The `pre-commit` hook runs before Git creates the commit and can be used for checks such as linting and tests.

chapters.title: Advanced Git Internals
chapters.summary: Explore Git objects, hashes, refs, HEAD, the index, packfiles, and the mechanics behind Git's distributed architecture.

sections.title: Git Objects
sections.content:
Git stores data using objects. The core object types are **blob**, **tree**, **commit**, and **tag**. Blobs contain file contents, trees describe directory structures, commits point to trees and parent commits, and annotated tags can point to Git objects with metadata.

Objects are addressed by cryptographic object IDs.

diagram.title: Git Object Model
diagram.code:
flowchart TD
  C[Commit Object] --> T[Tree Object]
  C --> P[Parent Commit]
  T --> B1[Blob: file A]
  T --> B2[Blob: file B]
  T --> T2[Subdirectory Tree]

codeExample.title: Inspect an Object
codeExample.code:
git cat-file -t HEAD
git cat-file -p HEAD
git cat-file -t HEAD^{tree}
git rev-parse HEAD
codeExample.explanation: `cat-file` can inspect Git objects. `rev-parse` resolves references such as HEAD to their object IDs.

keyTakeaways: Git stores content as objects rather than storing a sequence of file copies.
Commits point to trees and parent commits.
Object IDs provide stable content-addressed references.

interactiveQuiz.question: Which Git object stores file contents?
interactiveQuiz.explanation: A blob object stores file content. Tree objects organize blobs and subtrees into directory structures.

sections.title: Refs and HEAD
sections.content:
References, or refs, are names that point to Git objects. Branches and tags are examples of refs. `HEAD` is a special symbolic reference that usually points to the current branch.

This design explains why creating a branch is inexpensive: a branch is essentially a small reference rather than a copy of the entire repository.

codeExample.title: Inspect References
codeExample.code:
git show-ref
git rev-parse HEAD
git symbolic-ref HEAD
git branch --show-current
codeExample.explanation: These commands reveal references, the current commit, the symbolic HEAD target, and the active branch.

keyTakeaways: Branches and tags are references.
HEAD normally points symbolically to the current branch.
References make branch creation and movement inexpensive.

interactiveQuiz.question: Why is creating a Git branch usually cheap?
options: A branch is essentially a reference to a commit
interactiveQuiz.explanation: A branch is fundamentally a reference that points to a commit, so creating one does not require copying the project's files.

sections.title: The Git Index
sections.content:
The index is the data structure used as Git's staging area. It records the content that will form the next tree when a commit is created. Commands such as `git add` update the index.

Understanding the index explains why staging and committing are separate operations.

codeExample.title: Inspect the Index
codeExample.code:
git add src/app.js
git ls-files --stage

git diff
git diff --cached
codeExample.explanation: `git ls-files --stage` exposes entries in the index. `git diff` compares the working tree with the index, while `git diff --cached` compares the index with HEAD.

keyTakeaways: The index is Git's staging area.
`git add` updates the index.
The next commit is constructed from the staged index state.

interactiveQuiz.question: What does `git add` primarily update?
interactiveQuiz.explanation: `git add` updates the index with the selected content. A commit is created later from the index.

sections.title: Objects, Packfiles, and Storage
sections.content:
Git can store loose objects individually, but repositories commonly use packfiles to efficiently store and transfer many objects. Git can delta-compress related content to reduce storage requirements.

`git gc` performs repository maintenance, including housekeeping and packing objects when appropriate.

codeExample.title: Repository Maintenance
codeExample.code:
git count-objects -v
git gc
git verify-pack -v .git/objects/pack/*.idx
codeExample.explanation: These commands provide information about object storage and perform or inspect repository packing. Advanced storage commands should be used carefully.

keyTakeaways: Packfiles improve object storage and transfer efficiency.
Git can delta-compress related objects.
Repository maintenance is normally handled automatically or through standard Git maintenance commands.

interactiveQuiz.question: What is a major purpose of Git packfiles?
options: Efficiently store and transfer Git objects
interactiveQuiz.explanation: Packfiles consolidate objects and can use compression and delta storage to make repositories more efficient.

chapters.title: Professional Git Workflows
chapters.summary: Apply Git effectively in real engineering teams using trunk-based development, GitFlow concepts, commit conventions, protected branches, and CI.

sections.title: Trunk-Based Development
sections.content:
Trunk-based development keeps developers close to a shared main branch. Changes are integrated frequently, often through short-lived branches or directly behind appropriate safeguards. Feature flags can separate code deployment from feature activation.

The goal is to reduce long-running divergence and integration complexity.
keyTakeaways: Keep branches short-lived.
Integrate frequently.
Use feature flags when incomplete code must be deployed safely.

interactiveQuiz.question: What is a key characteristic of trunk-based development?
options: Frequent integration into a shared main line
interactiveQuiz.explanation: Trunk-based development emphasizes frequent integration into the shared trunk/main branch and minimizes long-running divergence.

sections.title: GitFlow and Release Branching
sections.content:
GitFlow is a branching model that traditionally uses branches such as `main`, `develop`, feature branches, release branches, and hotfix branches. It can work well for products with structured release cycles, but many modern teams prefer simpler trunk-based workflows.

The important lesson is not to follow a branching model mechanically. Choose the simplest workflow that fits deployment, release, and compliance requirements.
keyTakeaways: GitFlow is a workflow convention, not a Git feature.
Release-heavy products may benefit from dedicated release branches.
Simpler teams often benefit from trunk-based development.

interactiveQuiz.question: Is GitFlow built into Git as a special Git mode?
options: No, it is a branching workflow convention
interactiveQuiz.explanation: GitFlow describes a branching strategy implemented using ordinary Git branches and commands.

sections.title: Commit Message Quality
sections.content:
Good commit messages make repository history useful. A practical convention is to use a short imperative subject and add a body when context is required. Teams may adopt Conventional Commits such as `feat: add login validation`, `fix: handle expired token`, and `docs: update setup guide`.

The exact convention matters less than consistency and clarity.

codeExample.title: Examples
codeExample.code:
git commit -m "feat: add password reset flow"
git commit -m "fix: reject expired access tokens"
git commit -m "docs: clarify local development setup"
codeExample.explanation: These messages communicate the type and intent of the change and can also support automated release tooling.

keyTakeaways: Commit messages should describe intent.
Consistent conventions improve history search and release automation.
Avoid vague messages such as `update`, `changes`, or `stuff`.

interactiveQuiz.question: Which is the strongest commit message?
interactiveQuiz.explanation: The message clearly identifies both the category and intent of the change.

sections.title: Protected Branches and CI
sections.content:
Production repositories commonly protect important branches. Protection can require pull requests, successful CI checks, reviews, signed commits, or status checks before integration.

CI should validate important properties such as tests, linting, type checking, security scanning, and build success. Local hooks improve developer feedback but should not be the only enforcement mechanism.
keyTakeaways: Protected branches reduce accidental direct changes.
CI provides centralized and repeatable validation.
Server-side checks are more reliable than relying only on local hooks.

interactiveQuiz.question: Why should critical checks also run in CI if pre-commit hooks already exist?
options: Local hooks can be absent or bypassed
interactiveQuiz.explanation: Local hooks depend on developer configuration and can be bypassed. CI provides centralized validation for every relevant change.

chapters.title: Top Interview Questions & Practice
chapters.summary: Master 50+ essential Git interview questions ranging from core fundamentals to senior-level real-world scenarios.

sections.title: Junior Fundamentals
sections.content: Test your understanding of Git's core concepts, repository structure, commits, staging, branches, and everyday commands.
keyTakeaways: Understand Git's distributed model.
Know the difference between working tree, index, and repository.
Be able to explain common everyday commands.

interactiveQuiz.question: 1. What is Git?
interactiveQuiz.explanation: Git is a distributed version control system used to track changes and collaborate on software projects.

sections.title: Core Git Concepts
sections.content: These questions cover the fundamental objects and areas that make Git different from simpler version-control systems.

interactiveQuiz.question: 2. What does `git init` do?
options: Creates a Git repository in the current directory
Creates a branch on a remote
interactiveQuiz.explanation: `git init` creates the `.git` directory and initializes the current directory as a Git repository.

sections.title: Staging and Commits
sections.content: Practice questions about the staging area, diffs, commits, amend, reset, and restoring files.

interactiveQuiz.question: 3. What does `git add` do?
options: Updates the staging area with selected changes
interactiveQuiz.explanation: `git add` places selected content into the Git index, preparing it for the next commit.

sections.title: Branching Questions
sections.content: Test your knowledge of branch references, HEAD, switching, tracking, and branch lifecycle.

interactiveQuiz.question: 4. Why are Git branches lightweight?
options: They are essentially references to commits
They are stored only on GitHub
interactiveQuiz.explanation: A branch is essentially a reference pointing to a commit, so creating one does not require copying the project.

sections.title: Remote Collaboration Questions
sections.content: Test remote repositories, fetch, pull, push, upstream branches, and pull requests.

interactiveQuiz.question: 5. What does `git fetch` do?
options: Downloads remote updates without integrating them into the current branch
interactiveQuiz.explanation: `git fetch` downloads objects and updates remote-tracking references without automatically changing the current branch.

sections.title: Intermediate Git Questions
sections.content: Challenge yourself with merge, rebase, conflicts, stash, cherry-pick, tags, and history inspection.

interactiveQuiz.question: 6. What is the main difference between merge and rebase?
options: Merge deletes history while rebase preserves it
Merge combines histories while rebase replays commits onto a new base
Rebase only works with remote repositories
interactiveQuiz.explanation: Merge integrates divergent histories, potentially creating a merge commit. Rebase replays commits onto another base and therefore rewrites their identities.

sections.title: Advanced History Questions
sections.content: These questions focus on reflog, reset modes, detached HEAD, bisect, and history rewriting.

interactiveQuiz.question: 7. What is the main purpose of `git reflog`?
options: Record local reference movements for recovery
interactiveQuiz.explanation: Reflog records local updates to references and can help recover commits after resets, rebases, and other destructive-looking operations.

sections.title: Git Internals Questions
sections.content: Explore Git's object model, refs, the index, object IDs, and storage.

interactiveQuiz.question: 8. Which object stores the contents of a file?
interactiveQuiz.explanation: A blob stores file content. Trees organize blobs and subtrees, while commits point to trees and parent commits.

sections.title: Real-World Scenarios
sections.content: Practice practical situations that commonly appear in Git interviews.

interactiveQuiz.question: 9. You accidentally ran `git reset --hard HEAD~1`. What should you check first to recover the previous commit?
interactiveQuiz.explanation: The reflog records previous local HEAD positions. If the commit is still available, you can locate it there and create a branch or reset back to it.

sections.title: Senior Git Workflow Questions
sections.content: These questions cover team practices, protected branches, CI, history rewriting, and repository design.

interactiveQuiz.question: 10. Why should shared public history generally not be rebased casually?
options: Rebase changes commit identities and can disrupt collaborators
interactiveQuiz.explanation: Rebase creates new commit identities. If collaborators already based work on the old commits, rewriting them can create confusing divergence and require force pushes.

sections.title: Interview Question 11
sections.content: Core Git knowledge.

interactiveQuiz.question: 11. What does HEAD usually point to?
interactiveQuiz.explanation: HEAD normally points symbolically to the currently checked-out branch, which points to the current commit.

sections.title: Interview Question 12
sections.content: Core Git knowledge.

interactiveQuiz.question: 12. Which command shows unstaged changes?
interactiveQuiz.explanation: `git diff` compares the working tree with the index and therefore shows unstaged changes.

sections.title: Interview Question 13
sections.content: Core Git knowledge.

interactiveQuiz.question: 13. Which command shows staged changes?
interactiveQuiz.explanation: `git diff --staged` compares the index with HEAD and shows what is currently staged.

sections.title: Interview Question 14
sections.content: Core Git knowledge.

interactiveQuiz.question: 14. What does `git commit --amend` do?
options: Replaces the latest commit with a corrected version
interactiveQuiz.explanation: Amend replaces the latest commit, allowing you to modify its message or include additional staged changes.

sections.title: Interview Question 15
sections.content: Reset knowledge.

interactiveQuiz.question: 15. Which reset mode leaves changes staged?
interactiveQuiz.explanation: `git reset --soft` moves HEAD while leaving both the index and working tree unchanged.

sections.title: Interview Question 16
sections.content: Reset knowledge.

interactiveQuiz.question: 16. What does default `git reset` mode do to the index?
options: Resets it while keeping working-tree changes
interactiveQuiz.explanation: The default mode is `--mixed`, which resets the index while leaving working-tree changes intact.

sections.title: Interview Question 17
sections.content: Reset safety.

interactiveQuiz.question: 17. Why is `git reset --hard` dangerous?
options: It can discard tracked working-tree changes
interactiveQuiz.explanation: `--hard` resets HEAD, the index, and working tree to the target state, potentially discarding uncommitted tracked changes.

sections.title: Interview Question 18
sections.content: Merge knowledge.

interactiveQuiz.question: 18. When can a merge be fast-forward?
options: When the target branch is an ancestor of the source branch
interactiveQuiz.explanation: A fast-forward is possible when the target branch has no commits that are not already ancestors of the source branch.

sections.title: Interview Question 19
sections.content: Merge knowledge.

interactiveQuiz.question: 19. How many parents can a normal merge commit have?
interactiveQuiz.explanation: A typical two-way merge commit has two parents, one from each integrated line of development. Octopus merges can have more.

sections.title: Interview Question 20
sections.content: Rebase knowledge.

interactiveQuiz.question: 20. What does rebase primarily do?
interactiveQuiz.explanation: Rebase takes commits from one history and replays them on top of a new base commit.

sections.title: Interview Question 21
sections.content: Rebase knowledge.

interactiveQuiz.question: 21. Why do rebased commits have different hashes?
options: Their parent and commit metadata change
interactiveQuiz.explanation: A commit hash incorporates its content and metadata, including its parent. Replaying it changes its parent relationship and therefore its identity.

sections.title: Interview Question 22
sections.content: Conflict resolution.

interactiveQuiz.question: 22. What do `<<<<<<<` and `>>>>>>>` indicate?
interactiveQuiz.explanation: Git inserts conflict markers to show competing sections that require manual resolution.

sections.title: Interview Question 23
sections.content: Conflict resolution.

interactiveQuiz.question: 23. How do you tell Git a conflicted file is resolved?
interactiveQuiz.explanation: After editing the file into its desired final state, staging it with `git add` marks the conflict as resolved.

sections.title: Interview Question 24
sections.content: Rebase conflict recovery.

interactiveQuiz.question: 24. Which command cancels an in-progress rebase?
interactiveQuiz.explanation: `git rebase --abort` stops the current rebase and attempts to restore the repository to its pre-rebase state.

sections.title: Interview Question 25
sections.content: Interactive rebase.

interactiveQuiz.question: 25. What is interactive rebase commonly used for?
interactiveQuiz.explanation: Interactive rebase allows developers to reorder, edit, squash, reword, or drop commits.

sections.title: Interview Question 26
sections.content: Cherry-pick.

interactiveQuiz.question: 26. When is cherry-pick useful?
options: When you need a specific commit's changes on another branch
When you want to delete Git
When you want to rename all files
When you need to initialize a repository
interactiveQuiz.explanation: Cherry-pick selectively applies the changes introduced by one or more commits to the current branch.

sections.title: Interview Question 27
sections.content: Cherry-pick.

interactiveQuiz.question: 27. Does cherry-pick preserve the original commit hash?
options: No, it normally creates a new commit
interactiveQuiz.explanation: Cherry-pick applies the changes and creates a new commit, so its identity normally differs from the source commit.

sections.title: Interview Question 28
sections.content: Stash.

interactiveQuiz.question: 28. What does `git stash` do?
interactiveQuiz.explanation: Stash temporarily stores changes so you can switch context without committing incomplete work.

sections.title: Interview Question 29
sections.content: Stash.

interactiveQuiz.question: 29. Which command includes untracked files in a stash?
interactiveQuiz.explanation: The `-u` or `--include-untracked` option includes untracked files in the stash.

sections.title: Interview Question 30
sections.content: Remote repositories.

interactiveQuiz.question: 30. What is `origin`?
options: A conventional name for a remote
interactiveQuiz.explanation: `origin` is a conventional remote name, commonly created automatically when cloning a repository.

sections.title: Interview Question 31
sections.content: Remote repositories.

interactiveQuiz.question: 31. What does `git remote -v` show?
interactiveQuiz.explanation: `git remote -v` displays the configured remotes and their fetch and push URLs.

sections.title: Interview Question 32
sections.content: Fetch and pull.

interactiveQuiz.question: 32. What is the major difference between fetch and pull?
options: Fetch downloads without integrating; pull fetches and integrates
interactiveQuiz.explanation: `git fetch` updates remote-tracking references without integrating into the current branch. `git pull` normally fetches and then integrates.

sections.title: Interview Question 33
sections.content: Push.

interactiveQuiz.question: 33. What does `git push -u origin feature` do?
options: Pushes the branch and establishes upstream tracking
interactiveQuiz.explanation: The `-u` option establishes the remote branch as the upstream branch for the local feature branch.

sections.title: Interview Question 34
sections.content: Force pushing.

interactiveQuiz.question: 34. Why is `--force-with-lease` safer than `--force`?
options: It checks the remote branch has not unexpectedly changed
interactiveQuiz.explanation: Force-with-lease checks the expected remote state before replacing it, reducing the chance of overwriting another developer's unseen work.

sections.title: Interview Question 35
sections.content: Tags.

interactiveQuiz.question: 35. What are Git tags commonly used for?
options: Marking important commits such as releases
interactiveQuiz.explanation: Tags provide stable names for important points in history, commonly release versions such as `v2.0.0`.

sections.title: Interview Question 36
sections.content: Tags.

interactiveQuiz.question: 36. What is an annotated tag?
options: A tag containing metadata such as message and tagger information
interactiveQuiz.explanation: Annotated tags are Git objects that contain metadata and can point to another Git object.

sections.title: Interview Question 37
sections.content: History inspection.

interactiveQuiz.question: 37. What does `git blame` show?
options: The commit and author associated with each line's latest change
interactiveQuiz.explanation: `git blame` annotates lines with the commit and author responsible for the latest modification.

sections.title: Interview Question 38
sections.content: Debugging.

interactiveQuiz.question: 38. What problem does `git bisect` solve?
options: Finding the commit that introduced a regression
interactiveQuiz.explanation: Bisect performs a binary search between known good and bad commits to identify the likely regression-introducing commit.

sections.title: Interview Question 39
sections.content: Detached HEAD.

interactiveQuiz.question: 39. What happens when HEAD is detached?
options: HEAD points directly to a commit
interactiveQuiz.explanation: Detached HEAD means HEAD points directly to a commit rather than through a branch reference.

sections.title: Interview Question 40
sections.content: Detached HEAD.

interactiveQuiz.question: 40. How can you preserve commits created in detached HEAD state?
options: Create a branch pointing to the commit
interactiveQuiz.explanation: Creating a branch gives the detached commits a persistent named reference.

sections.title: Interview Question 41
sections.content: Git internals.

interactiveQuiz.question: 41. Which four object types form Git's core object model?
interactiveQuiz.explanation: Git's core object types are blobs, trees, commits, and tags.

sections.title: Interview Question 42
sections.content: Git internals.

interactiveQuiz.question: 42. What does a tree object represent?
interactiveQuiz.explanation: Tree objects represent directory structures and reference blobs and other trees.

sections.title: Interview Question 43
sections.content: Git internals.

interactiveQuiz.question: 43. What does a commit object point to?
interactiveQuiz.explanation: A commit points to a tree representing the snapshot and to zero or more parent commits representing its history.

sections.title: Interview Question 44
sections.content: Git index.

interactiveQuiz.question: 44. What is the Git index?
interactiveQuiz.explanation: The index is Git's staging area and records the content that will be used to create the next commit.

sections.title: Interview Question 45
sections.content: Ignore rules.

interactiveQuiz.question: 45. Does `.gitignore` automatically stop tracking an already tracked file?
interactiveQuiz.explanation: Ignore rules primarily affect untracked files. An already tracked file remains tracked until removed from the index.

sections.title: Interview Question 46
sections.content: Git hooks.

interactiveQuiz.question: 46. Why should important checks not rely exclusively on local Git hooks?
options: Hooks can be missing or bypassed
Hooks only work on remote servers
interactiveQuiz.explanation: Local hooks depend on developer configuration and can be bypassed, so important validation should also be enforced in CI or server-side checks.

sections.title: Interview Question 47
sections.content: Team workflows.

interactiveQuiz.question: 47. What is a major advantage of short-lived feature branches?
interactiveQuiz.explanation: Short-lived branches reduce the amount of time changes diverge from the main line, making integration and review easier.

sections.title: Interview Question 48
sections.content: Protected branches.

interactiveQuiz.question: 48. Why are protected branches useful?
options: They prevent Git from storing commits
They can require reviews and successful CI before integration
interactiveQuiz.explanation: Protected branches can enforce repository policies such as pull requests, approvals, and successful status checks.

sections.title: Interview Question 49
sections.content: Pull requests.

interactiveQuiz.question: 49. Is a pull request itself a Git object?
options: No, it is a hosting-platform collaboration feature
interactiveQuiz.explanation: Pull requests are provided by hosting platforms such as GitHub and GitLab and are built around Git branches and commits.

sections.title: Interview Question 50
sections.content: History rewriting.

interactiveQuiz.question: 50. Why can rewriting shared history be dangerous?
options: It changes commit identities that collaborators may already reference
interactiveQuiz.explanation: Rebase, amend, and reset can create different commit identities. Collaborators who already have the old history may experience divergence and require recovery steps.

sections.title: Interview Question 51
sections.content: Senior scenario.

interactiveQuiz.question: 51. A developer rebased a shared branch and force-pushed it. What is the primary risk?
options: Other developers may have references to the replaced history
interactiveQuiz.explanation: Other developers may have based their work on the previous commit graph. Replacing that graph can cause divergent histories and lost references if not handled carefully.

sections.title: Interview Question 52
sections.content: Senior scenario.

interactiveQuiz.question: 52. You need to apply one production bug fix from `main` to an older release branch. Which command is often appropriate?
interactiveQuiz.explanation: Cherry-pick is appropriate when one specific commit needs to be applied to another branch without merging all of the source branch's history.

sections.title: Interview Question 53
sections.content: Senior scenario.

interactiveQuiz.question: 53. A bug appeared somewhere in the last 500 commits, and you have a reliable automated test. Which Git feature can dramatically reduce the search?
interactiveQuiz.explanation: `git bisect` performs a binary search, and `git bisect run` can automate good/bad classification using a test command.

sections.title: Interview Question 54
sections.content: Senior scenario.

interactiveQuiz.question: 54. Your teammate says a commit disappeared after a reset. What should you recommend checking?
interactiveQuiz.explanation: The reflog records previous local HEAD and branch positions and is often the quickest way to locate commits after accidental history movement.

sections.title: Interview Question 55
sections.content: Senior scenario.

interactiveQuiz.question: 55. A team wants a clean linear history but developers frequently rebase local feature branches. What is a sensible policy?
options: Allow rewriting of shared main freely
Allow rebasing private/local branches but avoid rewriting shared history
interactiveQuiz.explanation: Rebasing private branches is generally safe because fewer collaborators depend on their commit identities. Shared branches should normally use non-destructive integration policies.

sections.title: Interview Question 56
sections.content: Senior scenario.

interactiveQuiz.question: 56. A developer runs `git pull` and unexpectedly gets a merge commit. What is a likely explanation?
options: The pull fetched changes and integrated them using merge
The repository was converted to SVN
interactiveQuiz.explanation: `git pull` commonly performs fetch followed by merge unless configured otherwise. If local and remote histories diverged, the merge can produce a merge commit.

sections.title: Interview Question 57
sections.content: Senior scenario.

interactiveQuiz.question: 57. What is the best reason to use `git fetch` before deciding how to integrate remote changes?
options: It allows you to inspect incoming history first
interactiveQuiz.explanation: Fetching updates remote-tracking references without changing the current branch, allowing developers to inspect and choose an integration strategy.

sections.title: Interview Question 58
sections.content: Senior scenario.

interactiveQuiz.question: 58. A repository accidentally contains a committed API secret. Is adding `.env` to `.gitignore` enough?
options: No, the secret must be removed from history and rotated
interactiveQuiz.explanation: Ignoring the file does not remove previously committed secrets. The credential should be revoked or rotated, and the sensitive data should be removed from repository history when appropriate.

sections.title: Interview Question 59
sections.content: Senior scenario.

interactiveQuiz.question: 59. Why should generated files such as `node_modules` generally not be committed?
options: They are large generated dependencies that can be reproduced from package metadata
interactiveQuiz.explanation: Dependencies such as `node_modules` can be recreated from package manifests and lockfiles. Committing them adds unnecessary size and platform-specific noise.

sections.title: Interview Question 60
sections.content: Senior scenario.

interactiveQuiz.question: 60. What is a strong professional Git workflow for a team using protected main branches?
options: Create a focused branch, commit logically, push it, open a pull request, run CI, review, and merge
interactiveQuiz.explanation: A focused branch, logical commits, automated checks, code review, and protected integration provide a controlled and auditable workflow while keeping the main branch stable.
